planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January for March transplanting. Bradley is a University of Arkansas release long popular across the Mid-South and Gulf South for its smooth, meaty pink fruit.

directions: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Bradley is a pink-fruited slicing tomato released by the University of Arkansas and grown widely across the Mid-South and Gulf South for decades as a reliable home-garden standard. The large, smooth, globe-shaped fruits have the mild, sweet, low-acid flavor typical of pink tomatoes, with meaty flesh and few seeds that make them excellent for fresh slicing and sandwiches. Plants are vigorous and produce well through the first flush of Southern summer heat, though yields taper once nighttime temperatures climb into the mid-70s like most standard hybrids. Stake or cage plants early and keep watering even to prevent cracking and blossom end rot through the swings between Gulf South downpours and dry spells. A good companion to a heat-set variety like Neptune or Phoenix for a longer harvest window into peak summer.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Panache needs long, hot summers to ripen its main crop fully and is best sited against a warm, sheltered wall in marginal areas.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, ideally sheltered from strong wind; Panache, also sold as Tiger Fig for its striking green-and-yellow striped skin, is a French heirloom fig grown as much for its ornamental fruit as for eating, with each ripe fig displaying bold longitudinal stripes over deep red, strawberry-jam-colored flesh. The breba (first) crop on old wood tends to be the more strongly striped and ornamental of the two annual crops, while the main crop on new wood ripens later in the season with slightly less pronounced striping. Fruit is sweet but not among the richest-flavored figs, so it is often grown as a conversation piece and fresh-eating novelty alongside more productive workhorse varieties like Celeste or Brown Turkey. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and control size, and protect young plants from hard freezes their first few winters, since Panache is somewhat less cold-hardy than common Gulf South fig standards.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Fig Fruit Facts
